answer: Sports arbitrage betting is covering every outcome of a game or market across different venues at prices that add up to less than 100% implied probability, locking in a profit of typically 0.5% to 3% whichever side wins. It works because sportsbooks, betting exchanges and prediction markets price the same event independently and move at different speeds. The math is simple; the business is speed, venue access and keeping accounts open.
intro: This is the long version: the kinds of arb, how the numbers work, where the opportunities come from, what the returns look like over a year, and which venues let you keep doing it.

blocks.p: Convert every leg to implied probability and add them. If the total is below 100%, the margin is 100% minus the total, divided by the total. On 47.6% + 50.5% = 98.1%, the margin is 1.9 / 98.1 = 1.94% of total stake.

Stake each leg as total stake x (leg probability / total probability). That equalizes payouts. If you would rather bias toward one side, because you think it is more likely or because one venue's rules are stricter, you can shift the split, but then it is a positive EV position with a floor rather than a pure arb.

Commission changes the arithmetic on exchange legs. A 2% commission on net winnings means a lay at 1.98 effectively pays out slightly less; use the venue's fee-adjusted price when you check the total. Prediction market fees are usually a few cents per contract and should be treated the same way.

list: Speed differences. Sharp money moves one venue, the rest catch up over seconds to minutes. This is the largest source and it never goes away.
Customer differences. A retail book heavy with public money shades favorites and overs; an exchange with no house view does not.
Structural differences. Prediction markets price in cents with no overround; sportsbooks add 4% to 5% of margin. The two disagree constantly by small amounts, and occasionally by enough to arb.
Attention differences. Props, alternates, small leagues and early-week lines get less trader attention and drift further apart.
Promotions. Boosts create prices unrelated to the event. They are arbs by construction and they are the quickest way to get limited.

blocks.p: A realistic operation turns over a multiple of its bankroll every week. With $50,000 spread across venues, $25,000 to $75,000 a week in matched legs is normal, at an average margin of 1% to 1.5%. That is roughly $300 to $1,000 a week before leakage from voids, partial fills and the occasional mistake, which together cost most arbers 10% to 30% of gross. Returns of 20% to 50% a year on capital are achievable; the triple-digit figures in sales pages assume unlimited access to retail books, which does not last.

blocks.callout: The capital constraint is real. Money has to sit at every venue in advance, which means a large share of the bankroll is idle at any moment. Venues that route from a single balance change the economics by putting the whole bankroll behind every leg.

takeaways: Sports arbitrage covers all outcomes at prices totalling under 100%; the margin is usually 0.5% to 3%.
Two-way, three-way, cross-market and middles are the main forms; bonus arbs are the shortest-lived.
Arbs come from venues moving at different speeds and serving different customers.
Realistic returns are 20% to 50% a year on capital, limited by venue access and idle balances.
Exchanges, prediction markets and sharp books are the durable legs; retail books are temporary.

faq.q: How much can you make from sports arbitrage?
faq.a: Margins are 0.5% to 3% per arb. On a $50,000 bankroll with disciplined turnover, 20% to 50% a year is realistic after leakage. Claims far above that depend on retail-book access that gets limited quickly.

faq.q: What is the difference between an arb and a middle?
faq.a: An arb guarantees a profit on any result. A middle backs both sides at different numbers so that both win if the result lands between them; otherwise you lose a small amount. Middles are a bet on the distribution, not a lock.

faq.q: Do prediction markets work for arbitrage?
faq.a: Well. Their prices have no built-in margin, they do not limit winners, and you can sell a contract to exit instead of betting the other side.
